## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds, so we have no signal. The budget is tiny: the default recipe gives 32 updates over 131k steps. The starting network can already, in principle, check whether a placement is correct: its footprint max/min/avg pooling can compare where a brick would land with the lowest missing target layer. So the likely bottleneck is how much it can learn in the budget, not what it can represent. Fewer PPO epochs buy more fresh samples (2 epochs gives 1.86x more, 1 epoch gives 3.25x), with about the same number of gradient steps when updates are smaller. Round 1 therefore tests the recipe on the starting network (2 epochs vs 1 epoch). The third candidate tests a structural idea: a head that scores each placement separately for each layer, so it can see directly whether the brick's landing layer matches the target. It uses the same recipe as the 2-epoch candidate, so that pair isolates the architecture effect.

### Round 2
All four runs scored exactly 0, both on dev and in training (train_success_last10pct is 0). That includes three recipes and the per-layer head, so neither more data nor that head has produced any signal yet. A likely cause is the reward. A sloppy placement still pays: a 2x2 brick that puts 3 cells in the target and 1 outside nets +2/N, while a clean 1x1 brick nets +1/N. The only reward for being exact is the +1 at the end, and with gamma 0.95 and a policy that never builds anything exactly, that bonus is almost never seen. So the agent probably settles on fast, sloppy filling. This round tests that idea. Raising gamma and lambda should carry the end bonus further back, and lowering entropy should make the policy more precise. I also test a per-layer head that adds learned 'anything missing below' and 'anything built above' features, which check whether a placement would seal cells underneath. Runs 1 and 2 use the same recipe, so they compare the two networks. Runs 2 and 3 use the same network, so they compare how strong the credit-assignment change should be.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and also 0 on training success in the last 10% of training. That covers recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, gamma up to 0.995, lower entropy) and per-layer heads that should be able to represent clean placements. If the dense reward worked as described, an agent placing bricks only inside target cells would sometimes finish small designs, so zero everywhere suggests a structural mismatch rather than slow learning. One candidate cause: the action layout may differ from the stated order (type, y, x), or y and x may be swapped. A fully convolutional head assumes that order and could not correct for it. This round tests that idea with three heads that can learn any action layout: (1) the baseline with a dense head added on top; (2) a pure MLP; (3) learned per-action queries that attend over cells. If all three still score 0, the action layout is probably not the problem.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, so there is no gradient to follow and no noise estimate beyond "all zero". The trials covered recipe changes (1 or 2 epochs, gamma 0.95 to 0.995), per-layer heads, a dense action head, a layout-free MLP and action-query attention. Failing every way suggests either that exact builds are out of reach at this budget, or that the world differs from its description in a way none of these designs exploited. The MLP's failure argues against a simple action-layout mismatch alone. The baseline's receptive field is shallow (two 3x3 convs) and its updates are few and large. For this last round I'm placing three different bets: (1) the baseline with many small, sharp, short-horizon updates; (2) a deeper fully convolutional ResNet whose head is a learned conv over each footprint window; (3) a small transformer that sees the whole grid, for ordering that depends on distant cells.
